claim: The Vegetative Health Index (VHI) has been used for decades to monitor drought across the natural range of Arabidopsis.
source: One such measurement, the Vegetative Health Index (VHI) has been used for decades to monitor drought, including in many places across the natural range of Arabidopsis (Kogan, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kogan, 1997

claim: Drought frequency during spring significantly predicts flowering time among Arabidopsis ecotypes (β = 50.016, p < 2×10−16).
source: We found that drought frequency during the spring (ß = 50.016, p < 2×10−16) and summer (ß = −28.035, p = 4.4×10−7) significantly predict flowering time among Arabidopsis ecotypes (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Statistical analysis with specific beta coefficient and p-value provided

claim: Drought frequency during summer significantly predicts flowering time among Arabidopsis ecotypes (β = −28.035, p = 4.4×10−7).
source: We found that drought frequency during the spring (ß = 50.016, p < 2×10−16) and summer (ß = −28.035, p = 4.4×10−7) significantly predict flowering time among Arabidopsis ecotypes (Supplementary file 2A).
evidence: Statistical analysis with specific beta coefficient and p-value provided

claim: 247 genes have LoF alleles significantly associated with drought timing and/or flowering time after accounting for population structure and multiple testing.
source: These analyses identified 247 genes in which LoF alleles are significantly associated with drought timing and/or flowering time after accounting for population structure and multiple testing (Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: Result from genome-wide association analysis with multiple testing correction

claim: When LoF genotypes were permuted, no genes were significantly associated with drought timing or flowering time.
source: In contrast, when we performed these analyses on a permuted LoF genotype matrix, we found no genes that were significantly associated with drought timing or flowering time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Control analysis using randomized data showing no significant associations

claim: Summer drought and earlier flowering associated genes overlap with spring drought and later flowering associated genes seven times more often than expected by chance (χ2=492, p < 2 × 10−16).
source: Together, summer drought and earlier flowering associated genes (Figure 2C), and spring drought and later flowering associated genes (Figure 2D) overlapped seven times more often than expected by chance (χ2=492, p < 2 × 10−16) and no shared associations were observed in the opposite direction.
evidence: Chi-squared test showing significant overlap between gene sets

claim: The strength of associations between LoF alleles and drought timing is strongly correlated with the strength of associations to flowering time (r2 = 0.48).
source: The strengths of the associations between LoF alleles and drought timing (P values) was also strongly correlated with the strengths of the associations to flowering time (r2 = 0.48. Figure 2—figure supplement 1E, Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Correlation analysis between two sets of association p-values

claim: When genotypes were permuted, associations between drought timing and flowering time were weakly correlated (r2 = 0.01).
source: In contrast, these associations were weakly correlated when genotypes were permuted (r2 = 0.01 Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), indicating that the result is not simply explained as an artifact of allele frequencies or by the relationship between drought timing and flowering time (i.e. Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Control analysis using permuted data showing weak correlation

claim: Plants are particularly susceptible to drought while flowering.
source: However, the observation both in nature and agriculture that plants are particularly susceptible to drought while flowering (Nam et al., 2001; Dietrich and Smith, 2016) has contributed to the longstanding hypothesis that adaptive flowering time should reflect patterns in the seasonal timing of drought events (Passioura, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nam et al., 2001 and Dietrich and Smith, 2016

claim: Locally adapted Arabidopsis thaliana populations begin flowering in their home environments just prior to and after periods of increased historical drought frequency.
source: Detailed studies of life history also reveal that locally adapted Arabidopsis thaliana (Arabidopsis hereafter) populations begin flowering in their home environments just prior to and after periods of increased historical drought frequency (Mojica et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mojica et al., 2016

claim: Early flowering genotypes in Arabidopsis are associated with low water use efficiency (drought escape strategy).
source: Flowering time in Arabidopsis is correlated with other drought tolerance traits such as water use efficiency and can serve as a proxy for alternative drought tolerance strategies, with early flowering genotypes being associated with low water use efficiency (drought escape strategy) and late flowering genotypes with high water use efficiency (dehydration avoidance strategy) (McKay et al., 2003; Lovell et al., 2013; Kenney et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to McKay et al., 2003; Lovell et al., 2013; Kenney et al., 2014

claim: Late flowering genotypes in Arabidopsis are associated with high water use efficiency (dehydration avoidance strategy).
source: Flowering time in Arabidopsis is correlated with other drought tolerance traits such as water use efficiency and can serve as a proxy for alternative drought tolerance strategies, with early flowering genotypes being associated with low water use efficiency (drought escape strategy) and late flowering genotypes with high water use efficiency (dehydration avoidance strategy) (McKay et al., 2003; Lovell et al., 2013; Kenney et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to McKay et al., 2003; Lovell et al., 2013; Kenney et al., 2014

claim: Loss-of-function alleles are overrepresented among alleles responsible for crop improvement.
source: In contrast to early theoretical predictions and popular assumptions, loss-of-function (LoF) alleles, those that eliminate or 'knockout' a gene's molecular function, are overrepresented among alleles reported as responsible for crop improvement and often produce adaptive phenotypes in wild species (Hoekstra et al., 2006; Rausher, 2008; Olsen and Wendel, 2013; Alonso-Blanco and Méndez-Vigo, 2014; Weigel and Nordborg, 2015b; Torkamaneh et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Loss-of-function alleles often produce adaptive phenotypes in wild species.
source: In contrast to early theoretical predictions and popular assumptions, loss-of-function (LoF) alleles, those that eliminate or 'knockout' a gene's molecular function, are overrepresented among alleles reported as responsible for crop improvement and often produce adaptive phenotypes in wild species (Hoekstra et al., 2006; Rausher, 2008; Olsen and Wendel, 2013; Alonso-Blanco and Méndez-Vigo, 2014; Weigel and Nordborg, 2015b; Torkamaneh et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: A number of individual genes exhibiting evidence of locally adaptive loss-of-function have been documented in Arabidopsis.
source: Indeed, a number of individual genes exhibiting evidence of locally adaptive loss-of-function have been documented in Arabidopsis (Grant et al., 1998; Johanson et al., 2000; Kliebenstein, 2001; Kroymann et al., 2003; Mouchel et al., 2004; Aukerman, 1997; Hauser et al., 2001; Mauricio et al., 2003; Alonso-Blanco et al., 2005; Werner et al., 2005; Barboza et al., 2013; Xiang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to specific studies

claim: Traditional genome-wide association scans based on the one-locus two-allele model perform poorly at detecting adaptive LoF alleles.
source: Unfortunately, traditional genome-wide association scans based on the one-locus two-allele model perform poorly at detecting adaptive LoF alleles, which because of the large number of mutations that can create them, are likely to arise through parallel molecular evolution (Pennings and Hermisson, 2006; Barboza et al., 2013; Kerdaffrec et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations and reasoning about parallel molecular evolution

claim: Adaptive LoF alleles are likely to arise through parallel molecular evolution because of the large number of mutations that can create them.
source: Unfortunately, traditional genome-wide association scans based on the one-locus two-allele model perform poorly at detecting adaptive LoF alleles, which because of the large number of mutations that can create them, are likely to arise through parallel molecular evolution (Pennings and Hermisson, 2006; Barboza et al., 2013; Kerdaffrec et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations and logical reasoning

claim: Genes identified with LoF alleles associated to drought timing and/or flowering time show parallel evolution of LoF.
source: As expected for genes harboring LoF alleles, these show parallel evolution of LoF and accelerated amino acid sequence evolution among Arabidopsis ecotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B, Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: Analysis of sequence evolution patterns shown in figures

claim: Genes identified with LoF alleles associated to drought timing and/or flowering time show accelerated amino acid sequence evolution among Arabidopsis ecotypes.
source: As expected for genes harboring LoF alleles, these show parallel evolution of LoF and accelerated amino acid sequence evolution among Arabidopsis ecotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B, Supplementary file 2C).
evidence: Analysis of sequence evolution patterns shown in figures

claim: Genes associated with drought timing and/or flowering time have similar global frequencies of LoF alleles compared to genes not showing associations.
source: While these genes have similar global frequencies of LoF alleles compared to genes not showing associations with drought timing and/or flowering time (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), they tend to have significantly fewer unique LoF alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) and greater frequencies of each independent LoF allele (Figure 2E).
evidence: Comparison of LoF allele frequencies between gene groups shown in figures

claim: Genes associated with drought timing and/or flowering time have significantly fewer unique LoF alleles compared to genes not showing associations.
source: While these genes have similar global frequencies of LoF alleles compared to genes not showing associations with drought timing and/or flowering time (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), they tend to have significantly fewer unique LoF alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) and greater frequencies of each independent LoF allele (Figure 2E).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D

claim: Genes associated with drought timing and/or flowering time have greater frequencies of each independent LoF allele compared to genes not showing associations.
source: While these genes have similar global frequencies of LoF alleles compared to genes not showing associations with drought timing and/or flowering time (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), they tend to have significantly fewer unique LoF alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) and greater frequencies of each independent LoF allele (Figure 2E).
evidence: Statistical comparison shown in Figure 2E

claim: The pattern of fewer unique LoF alleles but higher frequency per allele is consistent with theoretical predictions of adaptation by parallel molecular evolution involving recurrent mutation combined with positive selection.
source: This pattern is consistent with theoretical predictions and results from simulations of adaptation by parallel molecular evolution involving recurrent mutation combined with more rapid local fixation of alleles experiencing positive selection (Pennings and Hermisson, 2006).
evidence: Comparison to theoretical predictions from cited work

claim: LoF alleles identified were overwhelmingly associated with spring drought or later flowering rather than summer drought or earlier flowering (χ2 = 132, p < 2 × 10−16).
source: LoF alleles identified were overwhelmingly associated with spring drought or later flowering rather than summer drought or earlier flowering (χ2 = 132, p < 2 × 10−16, Figure 2).
evidence: Chi-squared test showing significant bias in association direction

claim: The bias toward spring drought/later flowering associations is consistent with the hypothesis that LoF alleles are particularly important in the evolution of phenotypic divergence.
source: Because the reference genome and gene models are from an early flowering Arabidopsis line, Col-0, this is consistent with the hypothesis that LoF alleles are particularly important in the evolution of phenotypic divergence (Rausher, 2008).
evidence: Inference based on reference genome characteristics and cited hypothesis

claim: Flowering time is strongly predicted by the accumulation of LoF alleles across the 214 candidate genes associated to spring drought and/or later flowering time.
source: We found that flowering time is strongly predicted by the accumulation of LoF alleles across the 214 candidate genes associated to spring drought and/or later flowering time (Figure 3A–E), estimating a 1 day increase for every three additional LoF alleles across these candidate genes (Figure 3F).
evidence: Regression analysis shown in Figure 3F

claim: Every three additional LoF alleles across candidate genes is associated with a 1 day increase in flowering time.
source: We found that flowering time is strongly predicted by the accumulation of LoF alleles across the 214 candidate genes associated to spring drought and/or later flowering time (Figure 3A–E), estimating a 1 day increase for every three additional LoF alleles across these candidate genes (Figure 3F).
evidence: Quantitative estimate from regression analysis

claim: The relationship between LoF allele accumulation and flowering time is best represented as a simple linear regression.
source: This relationship is best represented as a simple linear regression; the addition of a non-linear quadratic predictor variable did not significantly improve the fit of the model (F = 0.7005, p = 0.4028).
evidence: Model comparison with F-test showing no improvement with quadratic term

claim: 57 of 59 knockout lines in candidate genes flowered later on average than the wild type genotype (χ2 = 51, p = 8.045e-13).
source: As predicted by variation among Arabidopsis ecotypes (Figure 2D), the vast majority of knockout lines in these candidate genes (57 of 59, χ2 = 51, p = 8.045e-13) flowered later on average than the wild type genotype (Figure 3G, Supplementary file SF).
evidence: Experimental data from T-DNA knockout lines with chi-squared test

claim: LoF alleles identified include those previously linked to flowering time.
source: LoF alleles identified through these analyses and experiments include those previously linked to flowering time (Cui et al., 2007) and drought responses (Aghdasi et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: LoF alleles identified include those previously linked to drought responses.
source: LoF alleles identified through these analyses and experiments include those previously linked to flowering time (Cui et al., 2007) and drought responses (Aghdasi et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Groundbreaking yield increases during the green revolution of the 1960s were largely attributable to semi-dwarf phenotypes caused by LoF alleles in both rice and barley.
source: Groundbreaking yield increases during the green revolution of the 1960 s were largely attributable to semi-dwarf phenotypes caused by LoF alleles in both rice and barley (Spielmeyer et al., 2002; Jia et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Spielmeyer et al., 2002 and Jia et al., 2009

claim: Natural LoF alleles of the same gene in wild Arabidopsis produce similar semi-dwarf phenotypes as those in rice and barley.
source: Later it was found that natural LoF alleles of the same gene in wild Arabidopsis produce similar phenotypes (Barboza et al., 2013), suggesting the potential to mine ecological species for information directly useful for crop improvement.
evidence: Supported by citation to Barboza et al., 2013

claim: Crop losses resulting from droughts affect billions of people each year, posing the greatest threat to global food stability.
source: Understanding the genetics of drought adaptation in plants is particularly important as crop losses resulting from droughts affect billions of people each year, posing the greatest threat to global food stability.
evidence: Statement about the impact of drought on food security

claim: Drought stress can occur throughout the year and drought timing is forecast to change over the next century.
source: Drought stress can occur throughout the year and drought timing is forecast to change over the next century (Trenberth et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trenberth et al., 2014

claim: Dramatic evolutionary responses to drought events have been documented.
source: While dramatic evolutionary responses to drought events have been documented, (e.g. Franks et al., 2007), little is known about the relationship between drought timing and adaptation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Franks et al., 2007

claim: Little is known about the relationship between drought timing and adaptation.
source: While dramatic evolutionary responses to drought events have been documented, (e.g. Franks et al., 2007), little is known about the relationship between drought timing and adaptation.
evidence: Statement about knowledge gap in the field

claim: Drought timing remains a significant predictor of allele associations to flowering time when controlling for allele associations with latitude and minimum temperature (p < 2×10−16).
source: We found that drought timing remains a significant predictor of allele associations to flowering time when controlling for allele associations with latitude and minimum temperature (slope estimate in multiple linear regression, p < 2×10−16, Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: Multiple linear regression analysis controlling for confounding variables

claim: Most Arabidopsis populations exhibit a winter annual life habit, germinating in the fall and overwintering as a rosette.
source: Because most Arabidopsis populations appear to exhibit a winter annual life habit, germinating in the fall and overwintering as a rosette (Ratcliffe, 1961; Thompson, 1994; Burghardt et al., 2015), late flowering genotypes in spring drought environments are expected to still encounter drought conditions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ratcliffe, 1961; Thompson, 1994; Burghardt et al., 2015

claim: Delayed flowering may ensure that droughts co-occur with vegetative growth rather than during the drought sensitive reproductive phase.
source: However, delayed flowering may ensure that droughts co-occur with vegetative growth rather than during the drought sensitive reproductive phase.
evidence: Logical inference about the adaptive benefit of delayed flowering

claim: Late flowering genotypes have more water conservative water use and stomatal traits.
source: This pattern is also consistent with hypotheses explaining the more water conservative water use and stomatal traits observed in late flowering genotypes (McKay et al., 2003; Lovell et al., 2013; Kenney et al., 2014; Kooyers, 2015) and those from spring drought environments (Dittberner et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Genotypes from spring drought environments have more water conservative water use and stomatal traits.
source: This pattern is also consistent with hypotheses explaining the more water conservative water use and stomatal traits observed in late flowering genotypes (McKay et al., 2003; Lovell et al., 2013; Kenney et al., 2014; Kooyers, 2015) and those from spring drought environments (Dittberner et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dittberner et al., 2018

claim: The 2088 genes tested for associations to flowering time and drought timing are not a complete representation of LoF alleles in Arabidopsis.
source: It should be noted that the 2088 genes tested for associations to flowering time and drought timing are not a complete representation of LoF alleles in Arabidopsis.
evidence: Statement about limitations of the dataset

claim: Previously studied LoF alleles did not pass filtering steps primarily because the frequency or quality of LoF allele calls fell below filtering requirements.
source: In some cases, previously studied LoF alleles did not pass filtering steps (Supplementary file 3D,E). This was primarily because the frequency or quality of LoF allele calls in these genes fell below our filtering requirements (see materials and methods).
evidence: Explanation of why some known LoF alleles were excluded

claim: The Col-0 reference genome already has a documented LoF allele in some cases.
source: In other cases, the Col-0 reference genome already has a documented LOF allele.
evidence: Statement about reference genome characteristics

claim: LoF alleles are expected to be undetectable if they are the product of large insertions or deletions which cannot be properly identified with currently available resequencing data.
source: Finally, we expect LoF alleles to be undetectable if they are the product of large insertions or deletions which cannot be properly identified with currently available resequencing data.
evidence: Inference about technical limitations of sequencing methods

claim: The methods used are designed to minimize false positives (alleles classified as LoF, but which are actually functional).
source: Thus, while the methods used here are designed to minimize false positives (alleles classified as LoF, but which are actually functional), the likely occurrence of false negatives (undetected LoF alleles) in available data motivates the need for more sophisticated species wide genome sequencing efforts including a greater diversity of de-novo quality genomes for comprehensive detection of functionally relevant genetic variation across the species.
evidence: Statement about methodological design choices

claim: The likely occurrence of false negatives (undetected LoF alleles) motivates the need for more sophisticated species wide genome sequencing efforts.
source: Thus, while the methods used here are designed to minimize false positives (alleles classified as LoF, but which are actually functional), the likely occurrence of false negatives (undetected LoF alleles) in available data motivates the need for more sophisticated species wide genome sequencing efforts including a greater diversity of de-novo quality genomes for comprehensive detection of functionally relevant genetic variation across the species.
evidence: Inference about future research needs based on current limitations

claim: VHI was collected weekly since 1981 at 16 km2 resolution on a scale from 0 to 100, where values below 40 reflect drought conditions.
source: VHI was collected weekly since 1981 at 16 km2 resolution on a scale from 0 to 100, where values below 40 reflect drought conditions (Kogan, 1997) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Description of VHI data characteristics supported by citation

claim: The Vegetative Health Index combines deviations from historic climatic (Temperature Condition Index) and vegetative conditions (Vegetative Condition Index) to detect periods of ecological drought conditions.
source: This index is based on multiple data sources from NOAA satellites, combining deviations from historic climatic (Temperature Condition Index derived from AVHRR-based observations in thermal bands) and vegetative conditions (Vegetative Condition Index derived from NDVI) to detect periods of ecological drought conditions and distinguish between other sources of vegetative stress such as cold (Kogan, 1997; Kogan et al., 2005; Rojas et al., 2011).
evidence: Description of VHI methodology supported by citations

claim: The drought-timing index is equal to the natural log transformed ratio between spring and summer drought frequency.
source: Specifically, this index is equal to the natural log transformed ratio between spring and summer drought frequency.
evidence: Definition of the drought-timing index calculation

claim: More negative values of the drought-timing index reflect environments where drought frequency increases from spring to summer (summer drought environments).
source: More negative values reflect environments where drought frequency increases from spring to summer and are referred to here as 'summer drought environments,' (e.g. Figure 1B left).
evidence: Definition of index interpretation

claim: More positive values of the drought-timing index reflect environments where drought frequency decreases from spring to summer (spring drought environments).
source: Conversely, more positive values reflect environments where drought frequency decreases from spring to summer and are referred to here as 'spring drought environments,' (e.g. Figure 1B right).
evidence: Definition of index interpretation

claim: Genes were filtered to those containing at least 5% frequency of predicted frameshift or premature stop mutations and less than 5% missing allele calls.
source: First, genes were filtered to those containing at least 5% frequency of predicted frameshift or premature stop mutations and less than 5% missing allele calls from results generated by the 1,001 Genomes Consortium (1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016) using 'SnpEff' (Cingolani et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of filtering criteria used in methods

claim: Genes were filtered to those with a single predicted gene model to reduce instances where exon skipping might ameliorate LoF mutations.
source: To reduce instances where exon skipping might ameliorate LoF mutations (Gan et al., 2011), genes were filtered to those with a single predicted gene model (Lamesch et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of filtering rationale supported by citation

claim: LoF alleles were defined as those producing protein products with at least 10% lost because of late start codons and/or prematurely truncated translation.
source: LoF alleles were defined as those producing protein products with at least 10% lost because of late start codons and/or prematurely truncated translation.
evidence: Definition of LoF alleles used in the study

claim: Allelic heterogeneity expected to mask genes from traditional GWAS was corrected for by classifying all alleles as either functional (0) or non-functional (1).
source: Allelic heterogeneity expected to mask these genes from traditional GWAS (Remington, 2015; Monroe et al., 2016; Flood and Hancock, 2017) was corrected for by classifying all alleles as either functional (0) or non-functional (1).
evidence: Description of methodological approach supported by citations

claim: A final frequency filter of 5% global LoF allele frequency was applied, resulting in 2088 genes for downstream association analyses.
source: A final frequency filter was re-applied (5% global LoF allele frequency), resulting in 2088 genes for downstream association analyses (Supplementary file 3B).
evidence: Description of final filtering step

claim: Population structure was accounted for by performing a principal component analysis on the kinship matrix and including the first three principal components in each model.
source: Population structure was accounted for by performing a principal component analysis on the kinship matrix among all ecotypes and including in each model the first three resulting principal components, which explain >75% of variance in relatedness between ecotypes (Price et al., 2006).
evidence: Description of statistical method for controlling population structure

claim: The first three principal components explain >75% of variance in relatedness between ecotypes.
source: Population structure was accounted for by performing a principal component analysis on the kinship matrix among all ecotypes and including in each model the first three resulting principal components, which explain >75% of variance in relatedness between ecotypes (Price et al., 2006).
evidence: Result from principal component analysis

claim: P-values were adjusted to account for multiple tests by a Bonferroni correction.
source: The P-values (Pdrought timing) of the slope estimates (βdrought timing) for drought timing in these models were adjusted to account for multiple tests by a Bonferroni correction to identify those significantly associated (Supplementary file 3C).
evidence: Description of multiple testing correction method

claim: Flowering time was measured in growth chambers at 10°C under 16 hour days.
source: See Alonso-Blanco et al. (Alonso-Blanco and Méndez-Vigo, 2014) for details, but in brief, flowering time was measured in growth chambers at 10°C (considerably less missing data than experiment at 16°C) under 16 hour days.
evidence: Description of experimental conditions from cited source

claim: The expected number of co-associated genes under the null hypothesis of independent associations was 12, but 83 were observed.
source: Deviation from the null hypothesis of independent associations to drought timing and flowering time was evaluated by a chi-squared test (Expected number of co-associated genes = 12, Observed = 83, χ2 = 492, p = 2×10−16).
evidence: Statistical test comparing observed to expected overlap

claim: 122 genes in which loss-of-function is associated with drought timing or flowering time have orthologs identified between A. lyrata and A. thaliana.
source: To assess whether histories of selection for genes identified differ from the genome wide expectation, measures of amino acid sequence evolution were evaluated for 122 genes in which loss-of-function is associated with drought timing or flowering time and for which there are orthologs identified between A. lyrata and A. thaliana (Goodstein et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of dataset used for selection analysis

claim: The total number of unique LoF alleles differs significantly between genes associated with drought timing/flowering time and genes with LoF alleles but without observed associations (log10 transformed, p = 5.8×10−7).
source: To address the hypothesis that genes in which LoF alleles are associated to drought history or flowering time are likely to reflect positive selection compared to genes in which LoF are random with respect to drought history or flowering time, the total number of unique LoF alleles between these groups was compared using a two-sided students t-test (log10 transformed, p = 5.8×10−7, (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Statistical comparison using t-test

claim: The global frequency of LoF does not differ significantly between genes associated with drought timing/flowering time and genes with LoF alleles but without observed associations (log10 transformed, p = 0.11).
source: To control for the possibility that this result in an artifact of reduced frequency of LoF alleles in genes identified, the global frequency of LoF was also compared between these groups (log10 transformed, two-sided students t-test, p = 0.11, (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Statistical comparison using t-test showing no significant difference

claim: The frequency per specific LoF allele differs significantly between genes associated with drought timing/flowering time and genes with LoF alleles but without observed associations (log10 transformed, p = 3.4×10−7).
source: Finally, to further test the prediction that LoF alleles in genes identified have increased in frequency because of more positive selection, the frequency per specific LoF allele was compared between groups (log10 transformed, two-sided students t-test, p = 3.4×10−7, Figure 2E).
evidence: Statistical comparison using t-test

claim: LoF associations to spring drought are significantly more common than to summer drought (p < 2×10−16).
source: The significance of the tendency for LoF associations to spring drought/later flowering time (Figure 2D) was tested by chi-squared tests (spring drought vs. summer drought, p < 2×10−16; later vs. earlier flowering, p < 2×10−16, spring drought/later flowering vs. summer drought/earlier flowering, p < 2×10−16).
evidence: Chi-squared test showing significant bias

claim: LoF associations to later flowering are significantly more common than to earlier flowering (p < 2×10−16).
source: The significance of the tendency for LoF associations to spring drought/later flowering time (Figure 2D) was tested by chi-squared tests (spring drought vs. summer drought, p < 2×10−16; later vs. earlier flowering, p < 2×10−16, spring drought/later flowering vs. summer drought/earlier flowering, p < 2×10−16).
evidence: Chi-squared test showing significant bias

claim: LoF associations to spring drought/later flowering are significantly more common than to summer drought/earlier flowering (p < 2×10−16).
source: The significance of the tendency for LoF associations to spring drought/later flowering time (Figure 2D) was tested by chi-squared tests (spring drought vs. summer drought, p < 2×10−16; later vs. earlier flowering, p < 2×10−16, spring drought/later flowering vs. summer drought/earlier flowering, p < 2×10−16).
evidence: Chi-squared test showing significant bias

claim: The total number of LoF in candidate genes is correlated with flowering time (r2 = 0.39, p < 2×10−16).
source: To address the hypothesis that widespread LoF contributes to later flowering time phenotypes, the total number of LoF in candidate genes for each ecotype was calculated and the correlation between this value and flowering time evaluated (Figure 3F, r2 = 0.39, p < 2×10−16).
evidence: Correlation analysis between LoF count and flowering time

claim: A model including a non-linear predictor (squared value of total LoF in candidate genes) was not a better fit than the simple linear model (F = 0.7005, p = 0.4028).
source: We also tested whether a model which included a non-linear predictor (squared value of the total number of LoF in candidate genes) was a better fit than the simple linear model by an analysis of variance (F = 0.7005, p = 0.4028).
evidence: ANOVA comparing linear and non-linear models

claim: T-DNA knockout lines were generated by the SALK institute and exist in a common genetic background (Columbia).
source: These T-DNA knockout lines were generated by the SALK institute (Supplementary file 3F) and exist in a common genetic background (Columbia) (Alonso et al., 2003).
evidence: Description of experimental materials supported by citation

claim: Plants were grown under 16 hr of light at 20°C in growth chambers.
source: Plants were grown (59 T-DNA knockout lines, 10 reps of each line and 30 reps Columbia) in a stratified (by shelf), randomized design in growth chambers (Conviron ATC60, Controlled Environments, Winnipeg, MB) under 16 hr of light at 20°C.
evidence: Description of experimental growth conditions

claim: Flowering time was measured as days after planting to the emergence of the first open flower.
source: Flowering time was measured as days after planting to the emergence of the first open flower, based on the definition of flowering time used by the 1,001 Genomes Consortium (1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016).
evidence: Description of phenotype measurement method

claim: Knockout lines flowered significantly later than the wild type Columbia genotype (p = 8.1×10−13).
source: We tested the prediction that knockout lines would flower later (have higher lsmean flowering time estimates) than the wild type Columbia genotype by a chi-squared test (p = 8.1×10−13).
evidence: Chi-squared test comparing knockout lines to wild type

claim: Discovering adaptive LoF alleles is particularly valuable for inspiring targeted molecular breeding because functionally similar mutations can be mined from the breeding pool or generated directly by non-transgenic native gene editing.
source: Discovering adaptive LoF alleles is particularly valuable for inspiring targeted molecular breeding because functionally similar mutations can be mined from the breeding pool or generated directly by non-transgenic native gene editing.
evidence: Statement about applied implications of the research

claim: Satellite-detected drought histories and a functional genome-wide scanning approach prove useful for predicting the direction and molecular targets of phenotypic evolution.
source: Thus, satellite-detected drought histories and a functional genome-wide scanning approach prove useful for predicting the direction and molecular targets of phenotypic evolution.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the study's results

claim: Similar investigations with ecologically meaningful environmental variation could be valuable for discovering candidates underlying other important traits that are especially difficult to measure.
source: Similar investigations with ecologically meaningful environmental variation could be valuable for discovering candidates underlying other important traits that are especially difficult to measure.
evidence: Speculation about future applications of the approach

claim: The complex ecological reality of life history evolution processes is undoubtedly beyond the scope of this study.
source: These results provide new insight into the ecology and genetics of Arabidopsis life history evolution, but the complex ecological reality of these processes is undoubtedly beyond the scope of this study.
evidence: Statement acknowledging study limitations

claim: Other unknown climatic variables or environmental interactions and non-linearities likely contribute to flowering time adaptation.
source: However, other unknown climatic variables or environmental interactions and non-linearities likely contribute to the flowering time adaptation as well.
evidence: Speculation about additional factors not examined in the study

claim: Flowering time is only one component of phenology and other adaptive life history transitions such as germination timing may also be influenced by drought timing.
source: Flowering time is only one component of phenology and other adaptive life history transitions such a germination timing (Donohue, 2002) may also be influenced by drought timing and could change how drought timing affects the evolution of flowering time, a hypothesis that warrants further investigation.
